equity.level_reason: Race/ethnicity disparities are framed, quantified as rates 30%–40% higher and age-adjusted rate ratios, and interpreted. The only explanation offered is vaccination coverage, and no social, structural or political determinant is named.

level_alternative.reason: A reader could treat the vaccination-coverage disparity drawn from the National Immunization Survey as a structural explanation, but it is a proximate factor rather than a social determinant.

ev.q: Disparities in COVID-19–associated hospitalization among adults by race and ethnicity persisted during the study period
Cumulative hospitalization rates among AI/AN and Black adults were 30%–40% higher than were those among Hispanic and White adults.

These data suggest that racial and ethnic disparities in rates of COVID-19–associated hospitalization among adults continue but might have decreased since July 2021–August 2022.

equity.equity_measurement: Race-specific rates are age-adjusted from the catchment population. Other non-Hispanic races are omitted for small sample size, and table cells under 10 are suppressed.

notes: Rate ratios, percentages and the 88.1% vaccination figure depend on the direct age standardization and survey weighting listed under procedures. vaccine_outcome_type is null because vaccination status is a characteristic of hospitalized adults, not the primary question.
view_issues: Race ratios: 198.2/149.5 = 1.33 and 205.9/151.4 = 1.36, not the 1.4 and 1.3 stated. Sample: 1,754 - 350 excluded - 84 pregnant = 1,320, but the pregnancy exclusion is not stated. Text says 57.7% lacked the 2022-2023 dose; the table row is no dose of either formula. Age shares (13.5/16.7/21.3/48.6%) do not match the table's sample counts.
